content: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) is a condition characterized by the accumulation of serous fluid beneath the neural retina, which is associated with dysfunction of the choroid and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While the condition often resolves spontaneously, some individuals may experience irreversible vision loss due to progressive damage to photoreceptors or atrophy of the RPE. Various treatment modalities have been explored for CSC, including laser therapy, photodynamic therapy (PDT), and intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents. However, the relative efficacy of these interventions compared to observation or other treatments remains uncertain. Currently, there is no evidence-based consensus on the optimal management of CSC. Given the tendency of CSC to resolve on its own or follow a fluctuating course, observation is often the initial approach, though its safety and efficacy compared to active treatments remain unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of different interventions for CSC. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and clinical trial registries, was conducted without restrictions on date or language. The search included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing any intervention for CSC with another intervention or a control. The final search was completed on October 5, 2015. A total of 25 studies involving 1,098 participants (1,098 eyes) were included, with follow-up periods ranging from 16 weeks to 12 years. These studies were conducted across various regions, including Europe, the Americas, the Middle East, and Asia. Most trials were small, with fewer than 50 participants, and were often poorly reported, with unclear details regarding key methodological aspects such as allocation concealment. Many trials were not masked, and the quality of evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias and imprecision. The interventions studied included anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, bevacizumab), PDT (full-dose, half-dose, 30%, low-fluence), laser treatments (argon, krypton, and micropulse laser), beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Helicobacter pylori treatment, and nutritional supplements (e.g., lutein, Icaps). However, there were only one or two trials contributing data for each comparison, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Network meta-analysis, as planned in the study protocol, did not resolve uncertainties due to the limited number of trials and issues with intransitivity, particularly regarding acute versus chronic CSC. Low-quality evidence from two trials suggested that anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab or bevacizumab) were not significantly different from observation in terms of visual acuity improvement at six months in acute CSC (mean difference [MD] 0.01 LogMAR, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.02 to 0.03; 64 participants). All participants in these trials experienced resolution of CSC by six months, and no significant adverse effects were reported. Low-quality evidence from one study (58 participants) indicated that half-dose PDT for acute CSC may result in a small improvement in vision (MD -0.10 LogMAR, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.02), reduced recurrence rates (risk ratio [RR] 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.81), and less persistent CSC (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.02) at 12 months compared to sham treatment. No significant adverse events were observed. For chronic CSC, low-quality evidence from two trials (56 participants) comparing anti-VEGF agents to low-fluence PDT found little difference in visual acuity at 12 months (MD 0.03 LogMAR, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.15). However, there was some evidence suggesting that recurrent CSC was more common in the anti-VEGF group compared to the PDT group, though inconsistencies between trials made it difficult to estimate the effect. Persistent CSC at 12 months was more frequent in the anti-VEGF group (RR 6.19, 95% CI 1.61 to 23.81; 34 participants). Two small trials of micropulse laser treatment, one in acute CSC and one in chronic CSC, provided low-quality evidence suggesting that laser treatment may improve visual acuity (MD -0.20 LogMAR, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.11; 45 participants). No significant adverse effects were reported. Other comparisons between interventions were largely inconclusive. Twelve ongoing trials were identified, investigating interventions such as aflibercept and eplerenone for acute CSC; spironolactone, eplerenone, lutein, PDT, and micropulse laser for chronic CSC; and micropulse laser and oral mifepristone in trials where the type of CSC was not clearly specified. In conclusion, CSC remains a challenging condition to manage due to its natural history of spontaneous resolution in many cases and the lack of robust evidence supporting the efficacy of any single treatment. While several interventions have shown potential, the quality of existing studies is limited by small sample sizes, poor reporting, and methodological weaknesses. It is unclear whether treating acute CSC, which often resolves spontaneously, provides a clinically meaningful benefit. Future RCTs comparing individual treatments to the natural history of CSC are needed to identify promising interventions for head-to-head comparisons. Among the treatments studied, PDT and micropulse laser therapy appear to be the most promising candidates for further investigation in future trials.
